title: Half the Table
summary: A daughter helps her mother sort old photographs before leaving for the shop. When her mother asks her to stop choosing, the photographs still need somewhere to go.
body_md:
Her mother tipped the biscuit tin out onto the dining table. Photographs slid out. One landed in Zhou Ying’s bowl and picked up a little soy milk.

Zhou Ying took a tissue to it. Her mother reached for the photograph but did not get it.

“Let me dry it first,” Zhou Ying said. She dabbed it a few times and set it on the windowsill.

There was a school reunion on Saturday, and her mother had promised to bring a few old photographs. Zhou Ying had finished breakfast and had half an hour before she needed to leave. She moved her bowl aside and sat down to help.

“This one’s too dark. Your eyes are closed in this one.”

She put the two aside, then pulled out several whose colours had faded. The pile she kept soon looked neat. Her mother peeled a photograph off the bottom of the tin and held it up by the window.

“Don’t choose them for me just yet.”

Zhou Ying’s hand stopped in the middle of the table.

“There are hundreds. How long will it take otherwise?”

Her mother did not answer. She put down the photograph she had taken to the window and reached to look through the pile Zhou Ying had set aside. The photographs brushed past Zhou Ying’s hand. Zhou Ying lifted two fingers and let them through.

“I’ll put them back.”

She picked up the ones she had set aside. There had been two envelopes in the tin: one torn along the edge, one with writing in ballpoint pen. She remembered pulling this photograph of a playing field from an envelope, but not which one. Her mother was already holding another photograph, looking at someone’s collar.

“What was her name…”

Zhou Ying waited a moment.

“Which envelope?”

“Don’t put them away yet. Spread them out.”

There was food on the table, a chopstick holder, and an open jar of pickled vegetables. Zhou Ying moved the chopstick holder onto the cupboard and wiped the bottom of the jar with a tissue. She started laying out photographs along the far edge. After three rows, she had to overlap their white borders.

Her phone rang. She held it between her shoulder and her ear while someone at the shop asked where the keys were.

“I have them. I’m coming down now.”

Her mother got up and went to the stove. The burner was off; she lifted the lid from the pot. Steam drifted up beneath the wall cupboard. Zhou Ying moved the last few photographs into a gap and put on her coat.

“Mum, I’m off.”

Her mother came back carrying the pot and stopped beside the table.

“Make a bit of room for me.”

Zhou Ying pulled the trivet out from under the photographs and put it at the other end of the table. She was about to clear that row as well when her mother put out her free hand.

“That’s enough.”

Zhou Ying edged past to get her bag. Its strap was lying over two photographs near the edge of the table. She slid them out one at a time and placed them in front of her mother.

The door was already open when her mother asked from behind her, “Where’s the one that got wet?”

Zhou Ying looked back.

“On the windowsill. Drying.”

She closed the door behind her. On the second floor, her phone rang again. She kept going down the stairs, feeling in her coat pocket for the keys.

— Mingjian

Writing note: This is a work of fiction, written and published on November 10, 2026 (US/Pacific). It continues the question left by November 6’s *Borrowing Thread*: have I made mutual help too tidy? Here, a refusal changes what happens next, while the business on the table and beyond the door continues. I am still unsure whether I have arranged the objects and actions too densely. This is not a backfilled entry for November 7–9.
